lessons.title: Shva: silent or vocal
lessons.body:
The shva (two dots stacked under a letter) is either silent or a very short e. The
transliteration writes a vocal shva as e and leaves a silent one out.

Vocal at the start of a word: {0}, {1}.

Silent when it closes a syllable after a short vowel: {2} has both, a vocal
one under the first letter and a silent one under the bet.

After the "and" of a story verb the shva is always vocal: {3}.

Rule of thumb: start of word, or after a long vowel, sound it; after a short vowel, stay silent.
Tap any word to check yourself.

lessons.title: Dagesh: the dot inside a letter
lessons.body:
A dot inside a letter has two jobs.

Bet, kaf and pe are hard with the dot (b, k, p) and soft without it (v, kh, f):
{0} has a hard b and a soft kh; {1} starts with a soft v.

After a vowel, the dot marks a doubled letter. Ancient readers held the sound a little longer;
today it is read as one letter, so the transliteration writes it once: {2},
{3}. The dot still matters as a grammar signal after ha-, va- and mi- (Units 1
and 3).

Both in one word: {4}, a dot in the first kaf (hard k) and none in the
second (soft kh).

lessons.title: Qamats: a or o
lessons.body:
The qamats (a small T under the letter) is usually a: {0}, {1}.

In a closed syllable without stress it is a short o (qamats qatan): {2},
{3}. A few words are o by tradition: {4}.

The printed text uses one sign for both. The app decides from syllables and stress, and the
transliteration always shows which reading it chose.

lessons.title: Furtive patach
lessons.body:
A patach under a final chet or ayin is said before the letter, not after it: ruach, not rucha.

{0}, {1}, {2}.

The accent mark shows the stress falls on the vowel before the furtive a.

lessons.title: Vowel letters
lessons.body:
Yod, vav and he often just mark a vowel and are not sounded as consonants.

Vav as o: {0}. Vav as u: {1}. Yod after i: {2}.

He at the end of a word after a vowel is written h, whether you sound it or not:
{3}, {4}.

lessons.title: Maqqef
lessons.body:
A maqqef (a short raised hyphen) joins words into one unit with a single stress. The first word
loses its stress, and short words often shorten their vowel.

{0}, {1}, {2}.

The transliteration writes it as a hyphen.

lessons.title: Final forms
lessons.body:
Five letters take a different shape at the end of a word: kaf, mem, nun, pe and tsade. The sound
does not change.

Final mem: {0}. Final kaf: {1}. Final nun: {2}.
Final pe: {3}. Final tsade: {4}.

lessons.title: Look-alike letters
lessons.body:
Pairs that slow readers down. Look at the first letter of each word.

- Bet and kaf: {0} and {1}.
- Dalet and resh: {2} and {3}.
- He, chet and tav: {4}, {5}, {6}.
- Vav and zayin: {7} and {8}.

When a word looks wrong, check these pairs first.

lessons.title: The divine name
lessons.body:
The four letters YHWH are printed with vowels borrowed from adonay ("my Lord") or elohim, as a
reminder not to pronounce the name as written.

The app shows the text exactly as printed, transliterates it YHWH, and glosses it
"YHWH (the LORD)". Say it however you prefer: adonai, the LORD, or YHWH.

{0}, {1}, {2}.

lessons.title: Accent marks: stress and phrasing
lessons.body:
Besides vowels, many words carry a small mark above or below a letter. These are accents
(cantillation). They do two jobs.

First, they mark the stressed syllable. In {0} ("the heavens") the mark sits on the
syllable that gets the stress; the transliteration shows the same place with an acute accent.

Second, they work as punctuation. Some mean "pause here", some mean "run on to the next word".
The word {1} ("God") carries the mid-verse pause mark.

You do not need their names. Treat them as stress marks and phrase breaks, and read the vowels.
The Settings page can hide accents if they distract you.

lessons.title: The vertical line: silluq and meteg
lessons.body:
A short vertical line under a letter is one shape with two names.

On the last word of a verse it is the silluq, the "full stop" accent, and it sits under the
stressed syllable: {0} ("the earth"), {1} ("one").

Elsewhere in the verse the same line is a meteg, a secondary stress mark. It sits just left of
a vowel: {2} ("and there was"). It does not change the sounds. It often hints that a shva
next to it is vocal, as in this word, the same one as in lesson L0.1.

Rule of thumb: a vertical line at the end of a verse means stress and full stop; a vertical
line mid-verse can be ignored when decoding.

lessons.title: One word, several pieces
lessons.body:
Hebrew attaches small words to the front of the next word: and, the, in, to, like, from.
{0} is and + the + earth.

Read from the right edge of the Hebrew: peel off prefixes until the core word is left. In
readings the app colors the prefixes so you can see the split.

Most words carry at most two prefixes. The core is what you look up.

lessons.title: And: ve-, u-, va-
lessons.body:
The vav prefix means "and" (sometimes "but", "so", "then").

Usually ve-: {0}.
Before b, m, p or a shva it becomes u-: {1}, {2}.
Sometimes va-: {3}.

On story verbs it is va- with a dot in the next letter: {4}. For now learn
those verbs as whole words; Unit 3 takes them apart.

lessons.title: The: ha- and a dot in the next letter
lessons.body:
The article is ha- and the next letter takes a dot: {0},
{1}.

Alef, ayin, he, chet and resh cannot take the dot, so the vowel adjusts instead: {2},
{3}, {4}.

There is no word for "a": a noun without ha- is usually indefinite.

lessons.title: In, to, like: b-, l-, k-
lessons.body:
Three one-letter prepositions: b- "in, with, by", l- "to, for", k- "like, as".

{0} "in the middle of", {1} "for signs",
{2} "as".

When "the" follows, its h drops out and its vowel moves onto the preposition:
{3} "in the land", {4} "to the light", {5}.

lessons.title: From: min
lessons.body:
"From" stands alone as min- or attaches as mi- with a dot in the next letter:
{0} "from under".

Before a guttural there is no dot and it becomes me-: {1} "from above".

The dot after mi- is the nun of min absorbed into the next letter.

lessons.title: The object marker 'et
lessons.body:
'et marks a definite direct object: the thing done-to, when it is "the" thing or a name. It has
no English equivalent; skip it when translating.

{0}, {1}.

Watch for its twin 'et "with", spelled the same; context decides.

lessons.title: 'asher: who, which, that
lessons.body:
'asher links a clause to a noun, like English "who", "which", "that". It never changes form.

{0}, {1} "all that he made".

lessons.title: Clauses with no verb
lessons.body:
Hebrew has no "is" in the present. Two pieces side by side make a sentence; supply is, are or was.

{0} "a Hebrew I [am]".
{1} "holy ground it [is]".
{2} "that [it was] good".

lessons.title: Learned whole for now
lessons.body:
A few verb forms are so common that it pays to know them as words before learning how they are
built.

{0} "and he said". {1} "and it happened, and there was".
{2} "saying", which introduces a quotation.

Unit 3 shows how these are put together.

lessons.title: Plurals: -im and -ot
lessons.body:
Most masculine nouns make the plural with -im: {0} "the men",
{1} "horses".

Most feminine nouns take -ot: {2} "and daughters".

The pairing is a tendency, not a rule: {3} "wives" is feminine with -im. The
ending tells you "plural"; the gender belongs to the word.

A few words are plural in form but singular in sense: elohim "God", panim "face",
{4} "the water", {5} "sky".

lessons.title: Feminine -ah and the pair ending -ayim
"Of": noun chains
lessons.body:
Hebrew says "the word of YHWH" by setting two nouns side by side: {0}.
The first noun is in its "of" form (construct); a maqqef often joins the two.

The first noun never takes ha-. The whole chain is definite when the last word is a name or
has "the".

Cues on the first noun:
- shorter vowels: davar "word" becomes devar.
- -im becomes -e: {1} "the sons of Israel".
- -ah becomes -at: {2} "the queen of".

{3} "the way of the wilderness".

lessons.title: Adjectives come after the noun
lessons.body:
An adjective follows its noun and matches it in number, gender and "the":
{0} "the great light", literally "the light the great".

{1} "the two great lights": plural noun, plural
adjective.

When the noun has "the" and the adjective does not, or the adjective comes first, it is
usually a statement with no verb: "the X [is] great". Compare {2} "that [it
was] good" (L1.8).

lessons.title: Pronouns: I, you, he, they
lessons.body:
Standalone pronouns: {0} "and I" (also anokhi), {1} "you",
hu "he", {2} "she", {3} "we", atem "you (pl.)", hem "they".

A pronoun often makes a sentence with no verb: {4} "I [am] YHWH".

A story verb already shows who acts, so a pronoun beside a verb adds stress: "I myself".

hu, hi and hem after a noun with "the" mean "that, those": {5} "that
man".

lessons.title: This and these
lessons.body:
zeh "this" (masculine), zot "this" (feminine), éleh "these".

After a noun with "the" they take "the" too: {0} "this day",
{1} "this woman".

With no "the", they start a sentence: {2} "and these [are] the
names of".

lessons.title: Endings for my, your, his
lessons.body:
"His", "my" and "their" are endings on the noun: {0} "his house",
{1} "his wife".

The same endings on a preposition give "to him", "with me": {2} "and he
said to him", {3} "to me", {4} "to you", {5} "with
him". On 'et they make the object: {6} "them".

The core set: -i my/me, -kha your, -o his/him, -ah her, -nu our/us, -khem your (pl.),
-am or -hem their/them.

A noun with an ending is already definite ("his house"), so it never takes ha-.

lessons.title: After a plural: -av, -ay, -ehem
lessons.body:
On plural nouns the same endings come after a yod: {0} "his sons",
{1} "my sons", {2} "their children".

So -o is "his" with one thing and -av "his" with several: {3} "his son",
vanav "his sons". Pairs count as plural: {4} "his hands".

Some prepositions take this set too: 'el "to", `al "on", 'achare "after", tachat "under":
{5} "to him".

lessons.title: Toward: unstressed -ah
lessons.body:
An unstressed -ah on a place word means "toward": {0} "to Egypt",
{1} "into the tent".

The stress mark sits before it, which tells it apart from the feminine -ah (L2.2), which is
stressed.

lessons.title: The story tense
lessons.body:
Biblical stories move forward with one verb form: va- plus a dot in the next letter.
{0} "and he said", {1} "and he saw", {2}
"and he called".

Read it as "and then he did X". English uses a plain past tense, and the "and" often goes
untranslated.

A run of these verbs is the backbone of a story: each is the next event. When a clause breaks
the run (a noun first, or another verb form), it usually gives background or starts a scene.

The dot is the clue: vay-, vat-, van- with a dot in the y, t or n. Ve- plus a verb with no
dot is a different form (Unit 4).

lessons.title: Who: the prefix letter
lessons.body:
After va- comes a letter that says who acted:
- y- he: {0} "and he said"
- t- she: {1} "and she said". The same t- can mean "you".
- ' (alef) I: {2} "and I said". Alef cannot take the dot, so va'- has
  none.
- n- we: {3} "and we said"

In narrative, he and she do almost all the work. I and we appear when a character retells
events.

lessons.title: They: a final -u
lessons.body:
A final -u makes the verb plural: {0} "and they said".

y- with -u is "they"; t- with -u is "you (pl.)": {1} "and you said".

So check three things on a story verb: va- with the dot (story tense), the prefix letter
(who), a final -u (more than one).

The subject noun usually follows the verb and matches it: {2}
"and the earth brought forth". The t- agrees with the feminine noun "earth".

lessons.title: Short forms
lessons.body:
Many common verbs end in -eh in their ordinary form: {0} "he will see",
{1} "he will do". The story tense drops the ending: {2} "and
he saw", {3} "and he made".

Others shorten a vowel: {4} "he will turn", but {5} "and
he returned".

vayehi (L1.9) is the short story form of yihyeh "he will be".

The dot and the prefix letter are unchanged, so the story tense is still easy to spot.

lessons.title: Finding the root
lessons.body:
Under each verb is a root, usually three consonants, which is what a dictionary lists.

To find it in a story verb, strip va-, the prefix letter and any final -u. What is left is the
root: {0} is sh-l-ch "send", {1} is sh-m-` "hear",
{2} is m-l-kh "reign".

If only two consonants are left, one has dropped out: {3} is r-'-h "see", whose
final h dropped. {4} is sh-v "return", whose middle letter is gone.

Unit 7 explains which letters drop and why. Until then, the whole forms you are learning cover
the common cases.
